title: Public expectations of AI job loss and inequality are stronger in higher-income countries
source_unit: Pew Research Center Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey; 36-country public-opinion study with high- and middle-income comparisons
geography: 36 countries across high- and middle-income groups, including the United States

denominator.unit: adults surveyed across 36 countries; U.S. results come from separate 5119- and 3488-person surveys

job_loss_expectation_income_group.value: Median 55% in 18 high-income countries versus 36% in 18 middle-income countries say AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years
job_loss_expectation_income_group.unit: median percent by World Bank income grouping

uncertainty_income_group.value: Median 22% in high-income countries versus 34% in middle-income countries are unsure how AI will affect jobs

inequality_expectation.value: Median 35% in high-income countries versus 22% in middle-income countries say AI will increase the rich-poor gap; U.S. share is 46%
inequality_expectation.unit: percent or median percent saying AI increases inequality

u_s_youth_concern_change.value: Among U.S. adults ages 18-34, primarily concerned rather than excited about AI rose from 40% in 2024 to 55% in 2026
u_s_youth_concern_change.unit: percent of U.S. young adults in repeated survey comparisons

global_concern_excitement.value: Across 37 countries, median 37% are more concerned than excited and 41% are equally concerned and excited

observations.method: Comparative public-opinion survey with country samples designed to represent adult populations; income-group medians classify 18 high-income and 18 middle-income countries using World Bank lending groups.
observations.uncertainty: Expectations are perceptions, not forecasts or observed labor-market effects. Cross-country medians conceal within-country variation, and the U.S. repeated comparison uses different survey field periods and samples. Income classification is not a causal mechanism.
observations.subgroup: Adults by country income group, age, education, household income, AI awareness, and political ideology where measured.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher-income publics may be more aware of AI, more exposed to white-collar automation, or more willing to answer the question; lower uncertainty in middle-income countries may reflect awareness differences rather than optimism.

related_sources.claim: Detailed income-group comparisons for job loss, inequality, concern, and AI awareness.

boundary: This record adds a comparative perception-and-expectation layer for AI. It does not measure actual job loss, productivity, wage change, firm adoption, or whether concern becomes political action.
